strengths: First dedicated SWE-specific computer-use environment (VSCode-based, gymnasium-style API, Docker sandboxing, checkpointing) — fills a genuine gap between general OS/web agent environments (OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena) and tool-based SWE frameworks

PwP-Bench is broad and well-motivated: unifies 15 tasks across 8 languages, 4 categories (code gen/editing, multimodal synthesis, domain-specific, novel IDE/General-SWE tasks), with execution-based evaluation; Tables 1, 2, 5 position it clearly against prior benchmarks and tools

First systematic demonstration that computer-use agents can perform non-trivial SWE work in a unified interface, including a statistically significant win over a specialized tool-heavy agent on CTF tasks (McNemar's test, p=0.014)

The analysis section is a genuine contribution: well-illustrated failure modes (visual grounding, UI-state misidentification, linter-error blindness, inability to recover from suppressed actions) and an 'assisted' experiment that quantifies headroom from IDE tool use (e.g., rename tool: 0%→50%)
Practical infrastructure details (xdotool actions, DOM/extension-API state access, PwP-Bench-Lite subset) support usability and reproducibility; code and data are released
weaknesses: All headline results are on PwP-Bench-Lite with only 300 instances (20 per task); category-level scores in Table 3 rest on ~40-100 instances, so differences of a few points are noisy, and no error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported (the one significance test is only for the CTF claim)

No direct, controlled comparison with established tool-based SWE agents (e.g., SWE-agent, OpenHands, Agentless) running in the same environment; SoTA comparisons in Table 6 are imported from heterogeneous prior reports with different models, prompts, and compute budgets, weakening the central claim that computer-use agents 'approach or surpass' tool-based agents — the claimed superiority holds essentially only for Intercode-CTF

The 20-step iteration cap is restrictive for repository-level tasks and handicaps the computer-use setting relative to tool-based trajectories (acknowledged for SWE-Bench), making cross-paradigm comparisons potentially unfair in both directions

Averaging heterogeneous metrics (e.g., averaging 6 SWT-Bench metrics, linear normalization of Kaggle scores) into a single 'Overall Avg' obscures meaning and can produce misleadingly high aggregate scores

Claude-3.5 Sonnet dominates all results and is the only natively UI-trained model; conclusions about the paradigm are largely driven by one model, and possible data contamination (IDE/VSCode screenshots in training data) is not discussed

Presentation is rough in places: the release URL is blank, dangling references ('As shown in 2', 'Analysis 6.2', uncited footnote 1), Figure 6 caption contains OCR-like artifacts ('needs to 5x a bug'), and the write-up repeats the abstract nearly verbatim in Sections 1 and 2

Novelty is moderate relative to OSWorld/WindowsAgentArena: the main delta is IDE/SWE specialization plus curated benchmark aggregation; the two novel task sets (VSCode config, General-SWE) are small (20 instances each in Lite)
Reliance on closed-source frontier models limits reproducibility and longevity of the reported results

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: there is no SWE-specific environment for computer-use agents, and PwP's unified IDE-based observation/action space is a reasonable and well-motivated design.

The engineering is substantive: sandboxed Docker-based VSCode environment, checkpointing, gymnasium-style API, parallelized evaluation, and support for incorporating existing tool-based agents (Table 5, Appendix A).

PwP-Bench aggregates 15 tasks across 8 languages and multiple modalities (5400 instances), which is broader than prior SWE benchmarks, and the taxonomy of task categories (code gen/editing, multimodal, domain-specific, general-SWE) is sensible.

The analysis of failure modes (visual grounding, file editing, error recovery, inability to use IDE tools) is qualitatively interesting, and the 'assisted' experiment (Table 4) nicely quantifies the headroom from IDE tool use.
Honest caveats are included in Appendix C acknowledging that SoTA comparisons are not apples-to-apples.
weaknesses: Evaluation is too small and statistically fragile: results are reported on PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 instances per task (300 total), and some analysis is based on n=4 tasks (e.g., the rename task 0%->50% claim is 2/4 successes). Claims like 'surpassing state-of-the-art' rest largely on one dataset (InterCode-CTF, 100% vs 72% with n=20).

The central claim that computer-use agents 'approach or surpass' tool-based SoTA is overstated: the headline 46.8% average equals the previously reported SoTA average only via a heterogeneous macro-average of incomparable metrics, while the agent underperforms SoTA on most individual datasets (e.g., SWE-Bench 25% vs 55%, HumanEval 95% vs 98.8%, miniCTX 15% vs ~25%).

A 20-step cap severely disadvantages the pixel-based paradigm on repository-level tasks like SWE-Bench, undermining the fairness of the tool-based comparison; no experiment varies or justifies this budget.

The 'pure pixels' premise is undermined by the setup: non-Claude models receive Set-of-Marks annotations derived from DOM state, so the agents are not actually operating on visual perception alone, yet the paper frames the comparison as pixels vs. tools.
Only proprietary, closed-weight API models are evaluated; no open-source VLMs and no training/fine-tuning experiments, so the 'training agents to use IDE tools' thesis is asserted but not tested.

Novelty relative to existing environments (OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, TheAgentCompany, BrowserGym) is incremental — the paper itself admits these environments could express SWE-like tasks; the differentiating claims (SWE-specificity, checkpointing) are engineering refinements rather than conceptual advances.

Reproducibility is questionable: the code/data release URL in footnote 1 is literally blank, all results depend on closed APIs that change over time, and key experimental details (SoM parsing method, prompts, metric normalization for DSBench, etc.) are thin.

The macro-averaging of heterogeneous metrics (averaging 6 SWT-Bench metrics, linearly normalizing Kaggle scores, averaging CLIP-like scores for Design2Code) produces a single 'Overall Avg' number whose meaning is unclear and easily gamed.

Numerous presentation defects undermine confidence: '3.%' in Table 3, garbled Figure 6 captions ('5x a bug'), references to non-existent 'Figure 2' / 'As shown in 2', and incomplete footnote text suggest a rushed submission.

Poor results across the board (many cells at 0%) suggest the benchmark may currently be too difficult or poorly calibrated to be a useful signal for future work, and no human or simple-script baseline is provided to ground difficulty.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: PwP fills a genuine gap by providing the first SWE-specific environment for computer-use agents, and the paper clearly articulates the limitations of the tool-based paradigm.

PwP-Bench is impressively broad: unifying 15 task types across 8 programming languages and multiple modalities (5400 instances, plus a Lite subset) into a single task-agnostic state/action space is a substantial engineering and community resource.

The environment design is thoughtful: sandboxed Docker deployment, checkpointing for search/RL, a gymnasium-style API, multimodal observation support, and demonstrated compatibility with existing tool-based agents (Table 5) increase its usefulness as a testbed.

The analysis section is a genuine strength: systematic identification of failure modes (visual grounding, inability to exploit IDE tooling, lack of error recovery) with concrete qualitative evidence (Figures 7-13), and the 'assisted' experiment (up to 13.3% average improvement) provides actionable insight that IDE tool use is an untapped performance lever.

Honest reporting in places: the paper acknowledges confounds with prior SoTA comparisons (different budgets, 20-step limits) and includes a statistical significance test (McNemar's) for the notable Intercode/CTF result.
weaknesses: The headline claim that computer-use agents 'approach or even surpass' tool-based SoTA is overstated relative to the evidence: pure pixel-based agents achieve only 10.2% overall (Gemini/GPT models mostly near 0%), and the best result (46.8%) relies on file/bash API access, which is essentially a hybrid tool-based design. Only Claude-Sonnet performs well, so the generalization claim rests on a single model.

Evaluation is thin: only PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, 20 samples/task) is used, with some sub-evaluations based on as few as 10 instances (DSBench) or 4 tasks (rename experiment); no variance estimates or confidence intervals are reported, and only one statistical test appears.

The 20-step cap is a significant constraint for repository-level tasks like SWE-Bench, and comparisons against prior SoTA are acknowledged by the authors to be apples-to-oranges (different models, trajectories, budgets), weakening the 'first to show computer-use agents match SoTA' claim.

The evaluated models are already dated (GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5, Claude-3.5 Sonnet); given how fast the computer-use agent landscape moves (newer Claude computer-use models, OpenAI Operator), the conclusions about model limitations may not reflect the current state of the art.

Benchmark construction details raise concerns: macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics across 15 datasets (e.g., averaging 6 SWT-Bench metrics, linear normalization for DSBench) makes the 'Overall Avg' numbers hard to interpret, and task/source instance counts per category are not fully transparent.

Reproducibility is compromised: the release statement ('We release code and data at') is missing its URL, and implementation details of the modified VSCode codebase and DOM-state exposure are only sketched.

Presentation quality issues: several typos and broken text (e.g., '3.%' in Table 3, corrupted Figure 6 caption, 'Leged' in Table 6), and figures/tables referenced imprecisely ('As shown in 2'), which suggests insufficient polish for a top-tier venue.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to OSWorld/WindowsAgentArena: the main distinction is SWE-specificity of the IDE environment, and the conceptual framing (POMDP, primitive actions) is standard.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap: existing computer-use agent benchmarks (OSWorld, AndroidWorld, WebArena) focus on simple tasks, and this is the first comprehensive environment + benchmark for evaluating CUAs on realistic software engineering inside an IDE
Well-motivated research question with strong scientific framing: whether generalist CUAs can match specialized SWE agents, and what the key bottlenecks are (visual grounding, tool usage)

Extensive evaluation across many state-of-the-art open- and closed-weight models (9+ models), with a clean three-way design comparison (pure CUA, CUA + file/bash APIs, specialized SWE agent) that yields an actionable and interesting finding: two simple text APIs nearly close the gap to specialized agents (22.9% → 50.7%)

Rich qualitative and quantitative analysis (grounding error rates, function-usage distributions, assisted-tool experiments, long-horizon 250-step evaluations, error-recovery probes) that goes beyond just reporting headline numbers

Well-documented engineering: dockerized sandboxed VSCode environment, checkpointing for RL/search, gymnasium API, PwP-Bench-Lite for cheap evaluation, and thorough environment/benchmark comparison tables (Tables 2, 3, 5, 7)
weaknesses: Main evaluation uses only 20 instances per task (300 total in PwP-Bench-Lite), which is very small; results like 5% vs 10% differences on individual tasks are based on 1-2 instances, and several conclusions (e.g., CTF at 100% vs 72% SOTA) rest on extremely thin evidence with limited statistical support

Only one specialized SWE agent baseline (MiniSweAgent with a single model, Claude-4.0 Sonnet); comparisons against SWE-agent, OpenHands, or Agentless scaffolds, and comparisons of multiple base models for the specialized agent, would strengthen the central claim about generalist vs. specialist performance

Inconsistencies between main text and appendix undermine confidence: Section 5.1/Appendix F report grounding error rates differently (main text: 20% GPT-4o and 95% Claude-4.0; appendix: 20% Claude-4.0, 35% Claude-3.5, 95% GPT-4o), and some internal cross-references are wrong (e.g., 'see Section 5.1' pointing back to itself)

Macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics (SWT-Bench's 6 metrics averaged together, CLIP scores, normalized Kaggle scores, accuracy) into a single 'Overall Avg' conflates incomparable quantities and makes headline numbers hard to interpret

Evaluation is somewhat Claude-centric for the strongest results, and the file/bash-augmented design follows Anthropic's implementation, raising questions about fairness/generality of conclusions across agent scaffolds

Comparisons against 'best reported' specialized scores mix datasets of different sizes (20-instance subsets vs. full leaderboards), which the authors acknowledge but which weakens the significance analysis

Presentation issues: footnote 1 has an incomplete release URL, typos throughout ('potetntially', 'marco average', 'offciail', 'evluate', 'os steps'), and Figure 10 is explicitly 'not drawn based on relative size', limiting its informativeness

strengths: Introduces PwP, the first dedicated computer-use environment for software engineering with an expressive, IDE-based observation/action space, sandboxed Docker infrastructure, checkpointing, and a gymnasium API — a substantial and useful engineering contribution for the agent community.

PwP-Bench is broad: 15 tasks, 14 languages, multiple modalities (text, images, data files, PDFs), unifying 13 existing datasets plus 2 novel task sets, with 5400 instances and a convenient Lite subset.

Extensive evaluation across 9 models (open and closed weight, with and without UI-specific training) under three agent designs (pure CUA, CUA + file/bash APIs, mini-sweagent), including a 250-step long-horizon appendix experiment.

The core empirical finding — a large gap between pure visual interaction (22.9%) and API-augmented interaction (50.7%), approaching specialized agent performance — is clearly quantified and practically relevant.

Useful qualitative analysis of failure modes (visual grounding errors, hallucinated screen contents, failure to use advanced IDE tools, poor error recovery) with concrete examples and a prompted-experiment showing latent tool-use capability (25%→75% with rename hint).
Comparisons to existing environments (Tables 3, 5) and to best-reported specialized agent scores (Appendix E) are transparent about limitations and evaluation methodology.
weaknesses: Limited sample sizes undermine statistical reliability: main results use PwP-Bench-Lite (20 instances per task, 300 total), single runs with no error bars or confidence intervals, and some novel task categories (VSCode, General-SWE) have only 20 instances total, making category-level claims (e.g., 22.5% vs 37.5% differences) essentially comparisons of a handful of successes.

Novelty is mostly infrastructural: 13 of 15 tasks are ports of existing datasets, and the central finding (CUAs are worse through pixels than APIs; visual grounding is the bottleneck) largely confirms already-known limitations from web/OS agent literature, now reproduced in an IDE.

Metric aggregation is questionable: macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics (e.g., averaging all 6 SWT-Bench metrics, CLIP scores for UI mockups, linear normalization of Kaggle scores) produces 'Overall Avg' numbers that are hard to interpret and compare across tasks and against original benchmark reports.

Internal inconsistency in the reported grounding-error statistics: Section 5.1 states 20% (GPT-4o) and 95% (Claude Sonnet-4.0) of trajectories contain errors, while Appendix F reports 20% for Claude-4.0, 35% for Claude-3.5, and 95% for GPT-4o — a direct contradiction that needs correction.

The surprisingly perfect 100% on Intercode-CTF with Claude-3.5-Sonnet (vs. 72% reported SOTA with specialized tools) on only 20 instances raises concerns about task porting difficulty or evaluation fidelity, and the McNemar significance test on such small samples is not convincing.

The 20-step cap for main results is acknowledged as inadequate for SWE tasks; while a 250-step appendix exists, the headline numbers (Table 1) may understate all agents and the choice is driven by cost rather than task completion needs.

The 'assisted' experiment quantifying the headroom from IDE tool use is small-scale (hand-engineered tools, a few datasets, 20-instance subsets, 3 models) and the claimed 'up to 13.3% average gain' is loosely supported.

Potential contamination is not addressed: many ported datasets (HumanEval, SWE-Bench, Design2Code, etc.) are widely represented in training corpora, which confounds conclusions about genuine CUA capability on these tasks.
Writing quality issues throughout (e.g., 'Aas shown', 'marco average', 'offciail', 'evluate', 'intutively') and some analysis passages are redundant, suggesting the paper needed another careful pass.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: PwP is arguably the first comprehensive computer-use environment specifically designed for software engineering, filling a real gap between simple GUI benchmarks (OSWorld, AndroidWorld) and specialized SWE benchmarks (SWE-Bench). The environment design (VSCode in sandboxed Docker, xdotool actions, DOM/Set-of-Marks support, checkpointing, gymnasium API) is well engineered and the expressiveness arguments are convincing.

PwP-Bench is broad and diverse: 15 tasks spanning 14 languages, multiple modalities (text, images, PDFs, data files), and non-code SWE activities (IDE configuration, profiling, refactoring, debugging), with two novel task sets. The unified environment enables a like-for-like comparison of visual CUAs vs. tool-augmented CUAs vs. specialized SWE agents, which prior work could not do.

The headline finding is interesting and well-supported: pure visual interaction caps out at 22.9% while adding just two text APIs (file edit + bash) jumps performance to 50.7%, nearly matching the specialized mini-sweagent (48.8%). This cleanly quantifies the value of expressive visual interaction versus API access.

The qualitative and quantitative failure analysis is a genuine strength: systematic documentation of visual grounding failures (hallucinated screen contents, misidentification of UI elements, error recovery failure, memorized action sequences), the file/bash vs. computer-use action distribution analysis (Figure 6), the 'assisted' IDE-tool experiment showing up to 13.3% gains, and the 250-step long-horizon appendix.

Good reproducibility practices: open-source environment, pip install, PwP-Bench-Lite for cheap experimentation, detailed model versions/prompts/hyperparameters in Appendix D, and an honest discussion of limitations of best-reported-score comparisons.
weaknesses: Small evaluation samples create statistical fragility. Main results use PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 instances per task (300 total). Key claims rest on tiny counts: e.g., the refactoring finding (25% -> 75%) is based on 4 tasks (1 vs. 3 successes), and the General-SWE category has only 20 instances. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the main table (an exception is the single McNemar test for InterCode-CTF).

The macro-averaged 'Overall Avg' conflates fundamentally heterogeneous metrics (accuracy, averaged multi-metric suites for SWT-Bench/ChartMimic/Design2Code, CLIP scores, linear normalization against competition baselines). A single aggregate number across incomparable metrics makes cross-model and cross-category comparisons hard to interpret.

The surprising InterCode-CTF result (100% vs. 72% reported SOTA) is flagged but not adequately investigated. Given only 20 instances and possible differences in task setup, instructions, or verifier strictness versus the original benchmark, this outlier warrants deeper analysis or at least more caution, as it could indicate environment/verifier leniency rather than genuine agent capability.

Contamination and memorization are under-addressed. PwP-Bench ports well-known public datasets (HumanEval, SWE-Bench, etc.) that are likely in the training data of the evaluated models; the paper observes memorized action sequences but does not measure or control for data contamination, which could inflate or distort conclusions.

The 20-step cap for main experiments is a substantial limitation for SWE-style tasks; the issue is only partially mitigated by the 250-step appendix on three datasets. Cost-driven design choices shape the headline numbers, and the full 5400-instance benchmark is never actually evaluated.

The specialized-agent baseline is thin: only mini-sweagent with a single model (Claude-4-Sonnet). Stronger/contemporary specialized scaffolds are not compared under the same conditions, weakening the 'approaching specialist-level performance' claim.

The visual-grounding error analysis is manual, on only 20 trajectories per model, without a shared rubric or inter-annotator agreement, limiting the reliability of quantitative claims like '95% of GPT-4o trajectories contain a grounding error'.
